# Abstract

This gazetteer catalogues 471 urban, administrative, military and market settlements active across Joseon Dynasty Korea between 1392AD and 1910AD (covering 226.901 km² across the eight historical provinces). Synthesising historical administrative records from the *Sejong Sillok Jiriji* (1450AD), the *Sinjeung Dongguk Yeoji Seungnam* (1530AD), the demographic reconstructions of Kwon and Shin (1977) and Tony Michell (1979), and modern historical geographic inventories [@KwonShin1977Joseon; @Michell1979Fact; @March2024Gwon; @EberstadtBanister1992], the register encompasses every primary administrative node of the kingdom: the royal capital metropolis of Hanseong (Seoul, 241k), the former Goryeo capital of Kaesong (120k), the northern commercial hub of Pyongyang (95k), eight provincial capital yamen seats (*gamyeong*), 330 county administrative centres (*eupchi*), strategic coastal navy headquarters (*suyeong*), inland army garrison commands (*byeongyeong*), and emerging treaty ports and periodic market towns (*jangsi*). Across the 471 catalogued centres, the register documents 4.688 settlement-year population observations spanning 1392AD, 1450AD, 1500AD, 1591AD, 1600AD, 1650AD, 1700AD, 1750AD, 1800AD, 1850AD, 1900AD and 1910AD (averaging 9,95 temporal observations per site). At the 1750AD mid-eighteenth-century demographic peak, the leading urban centres of the kingdom were Hanseong (210k), Pyongyang (95k), Changwon (65k), Ulsan (56k), Daegu (48k), Jeonju (48k), Pohang (45k), Jinju (38k), Gyeongju (37k), Hamhung (35k), Suwon (35k), Andong (32k) and Gongju (32k). Alongside the 471 catalogued settlements, the regional source ledger records 13 excluded duplicate candidate entries out of 484 total evaluated entities.

# Background

Urbanisation in Joseon Korea was structured by the intersection of the centralized confucian administrative hierarchy and expanding regional agricultural and commercial networks [@March2024Gwon; @Kim2023Reconstruction; @Min2024Study]. Under the territorial governance system formalised in the fifteenth century, every administrative unit across the Eight Provinces (*Paldo*) possessed a designated walled or unwalled administrative seat (*eupchi*) that housed government offices (*dongheon*), royal guest houses (*gaeksa*), county confucian schools (*hyanggyo*), granaries and military armouries [@March2024Gwon; @Kim2023Reconstruction].

The royal capital of Hanseong occupied a unique position at the apex of the kingdom, containing royal palaces (Gyeongbokgung, Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung, Deoksugung and Gyeonghuigung), the supreme state council (*Uijeongbu*), the six ministries (*Yukjo*) and national altars [@Kim2023Reconstruction]. Hanseong was surrounded by stone battlements (*Hanyangdoseong*) and defended by outer fortress citadels at Bukhansanseong and Namhansanseong [@Kim2023Reconstruction].

Outside the primary capital, provincial administration was directed through eight provincial governors (*gwanchalsa*) stationed at provincial capitals (*gamyeong*): Gongju in Chungcheong, Jeonju in Jeolla, Sangju and later Daegu in Gyeongsang, Wonju in Gangwon, Haeju in Hwanghae, Pyongyang in Pyongan, and Hamhung in Hamgyong [@March2024Gwon; @KwonShin1977Joseon]. Along the maritime coasts, fortified naval commands (*tongjeyeong* and *suyeong*) guarded against Japanese piracy and western incursions, while army headquarters (*byeongyeong*) watched northern frontiers along the Yalu and Tumen rivers [@Yang2016Japanese; @Han2018Retrospective]. During the eighteenth century, rural periodic market towns (*jangsi*) operating on five-day cycles proliferated across agricultural plains, transforming local transport nodes such as Ganggyeong on the Geum River and Songpa on the Han River into vital commercial centres [@Min2024Study; @Shim2015Study].

# Methodology

Settlement records were constructed by extracting historical administrative seats from the *Sejong Sillok Jiriji* (1450AD) and subsequent dynastic geographic compilations, harmonised with longitudinal population records from Kwon and Shin (1977), Tony Michell (1979), and modern cadastral surveys [@KwonShin1977Joseon; @Michell1979Fact; @EberstadtBanister1992]. All 471 catalogued settlements carry geographic coordinates in WGS84 and assign to one of the eight historical provincial masks.

In the regional source ledger, 13 candidate records were excluded as duplicate historical aliases, close-pair suburban entities, or entities falling outside the spatial boundary of the Eight Provinces [@KwonShin1977Joseon]. For example, Miryang, Wanju, Gwangju, Janghang, Goseong, Heunghae, Mohyeon, Idong, Ganam, Daedeok, Jingeon and Byeolnae were consolidated into their respective canonical municipal entries to prevent double-counting of contiguous urban-rural populations, while Ulleung Island was excluded as an offshore oceanic entity outside the study area boundary.

# Testing and Validation

Ledger cross-checks confirm 471 included settlements and 13 excluded candidate entries (484 total evaluated entities, with zero unaccounted records). All 471 catalogued settlements carry verified geographic coordinates and documented longitudinal population records spanning the 1392AD to 1910AD period. Figure \ref{fig:sett-gazetteer} displays the rank-size distribution and the leading urban centres of the kingdom.

# Limitations

Two spatial factors affect urban population aggregation in this Joseon gazetteer. First, administrative centres (*eupchi*) in Joseon Korea typically encompassed both the walled administrative yamen compound and the surrounding civil agrarian wards (*myeon* and *ri*). Where historical records do not distinguish intramural inhabitants from contiguous suburban hamlets, figures represent functional administrative town populations [@KwonShin1977Joseon; @Kim2023Reconstruction]. Second, periodic five-day market towns (*jangsi*) expanded substantially during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, but frequently operated without permanent masonry walls; their populations are consolidated within their host county administrative seats except where distinct urban status emerged [@Min2024Study; @Shim2015Study].
